title: Deep Feedforward Networks (MLP)
subtitle: Contact session 5 · T1 Chapter 5 · non-linearity, forward pass, backpropagation, depth vs width and design rules

lesson.title: Why go deep: XOR
lesson.lead: A single neuron draws one straight line, so it **cannot** solve XOR. Stack layers with **non-linear** activations.

blocks.text: XOR's 1s lie on one diagonal and its 0s on the other: not linearly separable (Module 2).
**MLP fix:** 2 inputs → 2 hidden units → 1 output. Each hidden unit learns one line; the output combines them. In the hidden space, the points become separable.
h₁ = ReLU(x₁ + x₂),  h₂ = ReLU(x₁ + x₂ − 1),  ŷ = h₁ − 2h₂
blocks.caption: inputs (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1) → h = (0,0), (1,0), (1,0), (2,1) → ŷ = 0, 1, 1, 0 ✓

blocks.text: Why non-linearity?
f(ax₁ + bx₂) ≠ a f(x₁) + b f(x₂)
blocks.caption: the definition of a non-linear function

blocks.label: Key exam point
blocks.text: Without non-linear activations, stacked linear layers collapse into **one** linear layer: W₂(W₁x) = (W₂W₁)x. Depth adds nothing.

lesson.title: Activation functions
lesson.lead: ReLU is the default for hidden layers; sigmoid and softmax belong at the output.

head: Function
Formula
Range
Derivative
Notes
rows: Not zero-centred; vanishing gradients; use for binary output
Fast, no vanishing for z > 0, sparse; can "die"

blocks.label: Caveat
blocks.text: **Dying ReLU:** if a neuron's z is always ≤ 0, its output and gradient are 0 forever. Use Leaky ReLU, PReLU or ELU.

lesson.title: Architecture and notation
lesson.lead: L layers; layer ℓ has n_ℓ units, weights W⁽ℓ⁾ and biases b⁽ℓ⁾.

blocks.text: h⁽⁰⁾ = x,   z⁽ℓ⁾ = h⁽ℓ⁻¹⁾W⁽ℓ⁾ + b⁽ℓ⁾,   h⁽ℓ⁾ = σ⁽ℓ⁾(z⁽ℓ⁾),   ŷ = h⁽ᴸ⁾
blocks.caption: main deck: W⁽ℓ⁾ is n_{ℓ−1} × n_ℓ, rows = examples (H = XW)

blocks.text: Parameters = Σℓ n_ℓ (n_{ℓ−1} + 1)

blocks.label: Convention clash
blocks.text: The **numerical** deck writes z = W·a + b, with each **row** of W belonging to one neuron (W⁽¹⁾ is 3 × 2 for 2 inputs and 3 hidden units). The main deck writes hW with W as inputs × units. The maths is the same transposed: read the shapes in the question.
Output layer by task

lesson.title: Forward pass (numerical)
lesson.lead: Compute z, apply the activation, and repeat layer by layer.

lesson.title: Backpropagation
lesson.lead: Backprop applies the **chain rule backwards**, reusing each layer's error signal δ.

blocks.text: δ⁽ᴸ⁾ = ŷ − y   (MSE + identity, BCE + sigmoid, CE + softmax: all the same!)
δ⁽ℓ⁾ = (W⁽ℓ⁺¹⁾ᵀ δ⁽ℓ⁺¹⁾) ⊙ σ′(z⁽ℓ⁾)          ∂L/∂W⁽ℓ⁾ = δ⁽ℓ⁾ a⁽ℓ⁻¹⁾ᵀ     ∂L/∂b⁽ℓ⁾ = δ⁽ℓ⁾
blocks.caption: row-neuron convention; mini-batch form divides by B

blocks.text: W ← W − η ∂L/∂W,     b ← b − η ∂L/∂b
Why it's efficient

A naive approach needs one forward pass **per parameter**. Backprop needs one forward and one backward pass in total, about 2× the cost of a forward pass. That's dynamic programming with the chain rule.

blocks.label: Notice
blocks.text: The dead neuron's weights (row 2 of W⁽¹⁾ and column 2 of W⁽²⁾) **don't change**: its gradient is 0.

lesson.title: Losses and their derivatives
lesson.lead: Know each loss's derivative with respect to ŷ.

blocks.text: Examples: MSE with y = 3, ŷ = 5 → ℓ = 2, slope +2; y = 8, ŷ = 5 → ℓ = 4.5, slope −3. BCE with y = 1: ŷ = 0.9 → ℓ = 0.105, slope −1.11; ŷ = 0.1 → ℓ = 2.303, slope −10.

blocks.label: Derivations
blocks.text: Sigmoid derivative derivation: σ′ = e⁻ᶻ/(1 + e⁻ᶻ)² = σ(1 − σ). Tanh: tanh′ = 1 − tanh² (max 1, which is 4× the sigmoid's 0.25).

lesson.title: Vanishing and exploding gradients
lesson.lead: Gradients are products across layers, so they can shrink or blow up **exponentially** with depth.

blocks.text: Example: 4 sigmoid layers, ‖W‖ = 0.8, g′ = 0.25 (its maximum). Each step multiplies by 0.2: δ⁽⁴⁾ = 1 → δ⁽³⁾ = 0.2 → δ⁽²⁾ = 0.04 → δ⁽¹⁾ = **0.008** (0.8% of the original).

head: Problem
Fix
rows: Gradient clipping, proper initialisation, smaller η

lesson.title: Depth vs width
lesson.lead: Depth learns **hierarchical** features; width adds parallel features in one layer.

items: Deep: low-level (edges) → mid-level (shapes, parts) → high-level (objects). More expressive per parameter, generalises better.
Wide: more parallel features and higher capacity per layer, with a risk of overfitting.

blocks.label: Key theorem
blocks.text: **Universal approximation theorem** (Cybenko; Hornik, 1989): one hidden layer with enough neurons can approximate any continuous function on a compact set. But it may need exponentially many units. Deep networks do it with far fewer parameters.
Start with 2–3 hidden layers of 10–100 units. Use ReLU in hidden layers and a task-specific output.

lesson.title: Sizing a network (design rules)
lesson.lead: The numerical deck uses two rough rules to keep a network from overfitting.

blocks.text: L ≤ log₂(M / (d × c)) + 1          parameters ≤ M / 5
blocks.caption: M = training samples, d = features, c = classes

blocks.text: Final recommendation: **[20, 6, 3]** with regularisation. For d = 1000, M = 50,000, c = 5: L ≤ log₂(10) + 1 ≈ 4.3 → [1000, 512, 256, 128, 5] ≈ 675K parameters with batch norm and dropout.
Diagnosing training

head: Symptom
Fix
rows: Lower η, check gradients, normalise inputs

worked.title: Backward pass and update

problem.text: Same network, target y = (1, 0), BCE averaged over the 2 outputs, α = 0.1. Find L, all gradients and the new parameters.

worked.answer: L = 0.560; the dead hidden neuron receives no update. Check every number in the Lab bench.

worked.title: Gradient flow through 4 sigmoid layers

problem.text: ‖W⁽ˡ⁾‖ = 0.8 and g′ = 0.25 at every layer; |δ⁽⁴⁾| = 1. Find |δ⁽³⁾|, |δ⁽²⁾|, |δ⁽¹⁾|.

worked.answer: 0.2, 0.04, 0.008: the first layer gets 0.8% of the signal (the vanishing gradient problem). With ReLU (g′ = 1) the factor would be 0.8.

worked.title: Activations and derivatives at a vector

problem.text: z = (2.0, −1.5, 0.8, −0.3). Compute sigmoid, tanh and ReLU, and their derivatives.

worked.answer: Note how small σ′ is everywhere (≤ 0.25), while tanh′ reaches 0.915 near 0.
